# Infection and Sterility
An infection is a wound that never heals by itself. Left alone it gets worse tier by tier and poisons the patient. Dirty surgery and untreated open wounds cause it.
## Dirty tools Surgical tools and gloves carry a dirtiness from 0 (sterile) to 100. Examine an item to see how clean it looks, and whether it carries traces of other patients' blood.
- Every surgery step adds 4 dirt to each tool used and to the surgeon's gloves, and leaves the patient's DNA on them. - Operating without gloves counts as 25 extra dirt, and without a mask 10 extra. - Every [italic]other[/italic] patient whose DNA is still on your tools or gloves counts as 60 extra dirt.
Add it all up for one operation: - [bold]Over 40 total:[/bold] each step poisons the patient, more the dirtier it is (up to 12 per step). - [bold]Over 30 total:[/bold] each step can also infect the patient. The chance is 1% per point above 30, at most 90%.
You will be warned: [italic]"Your dirty tools and gloves are making the patient sick!"[/italic]
## Cleaning up Hold [bold]soap[/bold] and click the dirty tool or gloves, or use the [bold]Sanitize[/bold] verb on it. Each wipe takes 3 seconds and removes 25 dirt and one patient's DNA, and it repeats until the item is clean. You need a free hand, and moving interrupts it.
## Open wounds An untreated Laceration, Puncture or Burn of tier 2 or worse can become infected, a small chance every 5 seconds (0.4%, 0.5% and 0.3% per tier). Fractures and bleeding do not cause infections. A patient can only have one infection at a time.
## How an infection progresses - [bold]Early Infection[/bold] (tier 1): no symptoms. Lasts 150 seconds. - [bold]Spreading Infection[/bold] (tier 2): poisons the patient slowly. Lasts 150 seconds. - [bold]Septic Infection[/bold] (tier 3): poisons the patient faster and slows them to 80% speed. It is as bad as it gets.
The patient looks flushed, then feverish, then gravely ill when examined. A health analyzer tells you if they are infected.
## Strains Every infection is caused by one of three bacteria. Which one is chance, weighted by how it started: - [bold]Staphylococcus[/bold]: the common one after dirty surgery and cuts. Cured by [bold]cloxacillin[/bold]. - [bold]Streptococcus[/bold]: likelier from stab wounds. Cured by [bold]penicillin[/bold]. - [bold]Pseudomonas[/bold]: rare after surgery, but the usual one in burns. Cured by [bold]ciprofloxacin[/bold].
The strain is not shown by either health analyzer. Find it with the [bold]blood culture analyzer[/bold]: put a container with the patient's blood in it (draw it with a syringe) and, with Diagnostics training, wait 5 seconds for a printed report. The patient must still be around to be matched to the blood.
Take the report to an [bold]antibiotic synthesizer[/bold] to program it, then put in a container of Antibiox. With Chemistry training, it turns all the Antibiox in the container into the narrow-spectrum drug for that strain, unit for unit. You can build both machines from boards printed at a medical techfab.
The right narrow-spectrum drug in the blood wins the infection back one tier every 45 seconds and cures it from tier 1. While it works the infection cannot get worse and its symptoms are suppressed. The wrong one does nothing. Like Antibiox, 16 units or more is an overdose that poisons the patient.
## Treating it [bold]Broad-spectrum antibiotics hold an infection back but do not cure it.[/bold] The [bold]Drain Infection[/bold] surgery cures it: after an incision, lance the infected tissue with a scalpel, drain it with a hemostat, and cauterize the wound with a cautery. Draining needs a [bold]container[/bold], like a beaker, in your other hand to catch the exudate (30 units) that comes out; a full container will not do.
Dolls are drained the same way once their shell is off. Slimes have no flesh to lance: [bold]Purge Contaminated Jelly[/bold] siphons the infected jelly into a container with a hemostat, then coagulates the rest with a cautery.
While antibiox is in the blood: - New infections are blocked. - An existing infection is frozen at its current tier and its symptoms are suppressed. It carries on when the drug wears off. - The drug wipes out gut bacteria, leaving the patient with less stamina while it works and for a while afterwards.
[color=red]Overdose (16 units or more):[/color] the patient is poisoned (a double dose is painful but not deadly by itself), the protection is lost, a new infection from dirty surgery or open wounds becomes about three times as likely, and any infection escalates about three times faster. Do not double up on doses.
The [bold]antibiox auto-injector[/bold] holds a single 15 unit dose, just under the overdose line. It is stocked in the NanoMed Civilian vending machines and in the toxin first aid kit.
